title: Newton's second law and free-body diagrams
explanation:
Push a shopping cart harder and it speeds up faster; load it with bricks and the same push does less. OpenStax states both intuitions: acceleration is directly proportional to, and in the same direction as, the net external force [1], and inversely proportional to the mass [2]. Together: $a=\frac{F_{net}}{m}$, or $F_{net}=m\,a$.

The word *net* is the whole game. Draw a **free-body diagram**: the object as a dot, with every force acting on it as an arrow [3]. Choose a positive direction for each axis, then add the components with signs. Forces that cancel produce no acceleration along that axis.

Only forces *on* the object go in its diagram. Forces it exerts on other things belong in their diagrams.
keyIdeas: $F_{net}=m\,a$: acceleration follows the net force and shrinks with mass.
Draw every force on the object; add components with signs.
Balanced forces on an axis mean zero acceleration on that axis.

workedExample.problem: A $4$ kg sled is pulled right with $25$ N while a rope pulls it left with $5$ N (no friction). Find its acceleration.
steps: Free-body diagram (horizontal): 25 N to the right, 5 N to the left. Take right as positive.
Net force: $F_{net}=25-5=20$ N, to the right.
Direction check: the larger pull points right, and so does $a$.

pitfalls: Using one force instead of the net force in $F=ma$.
Adding force magnitudes without signs when forces point opposite ways.
Putting forces the object exerts on others into its own free-body diagram.

citations.quote: It seems reasonable that acceleration would be directly proportional to and in the same direction as the net external force acting on a system.
It also seems reasonable that acceleration should be inversely proportional to the mass of the system.
The free-body diagram shows all of the forces acting on the system of interest.
